article_title: Pedagogy Is for Kids: Andragogy Is for Adults
citation: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults.
title: Use a transactional approach to methods, timing, and content with adult learners rather than assigning full responsibility to the teacher
description: The essay reports that Knowles "properly rejects the common pedagogical practice of assigning full responsibility to the teacher for methods, timing and content, and recommends a more transactional approach for andragogy." Under this approach, decisions about how, when, and what to learn are negotiated with learners rather than imposed, and the transactional approach should include addressing the learner's need to know from the beginning.
requirements: Willingness of the facilitator to share responsibility for methods, timing, and content decisions with adult learners
constraints: The essay frames this as most characteristic of andragogy with adults; children are described as more trusting of teachers and more likely to accept teacher-directed arrangements
target_learners: adult learners
target_learning_goals: learner motivation and ownership of the learning experience
examples: Knowles' recommendation, cited from his 1998 work (p. 72), that facilitators adopt a transactional rather than teacher-assigned approach
key_sources: Moberg, E. (2006). Pedagogy is for Kids: Andragogy is for Adults. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED507785

article_title: Early Steps
citation: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Staff one-to-one tutoring with trained school staff rather than community volunteers
description: The program specifies that "Classroom teachers, reading teachers, or well-prepared paraprofessionals are needed to serve as tutors," while "Community volunteers are not suggested as tutors." Tutoring quality is treated as depending on staff who receive extensive training, observation, and feedback, so schools implementing one-to-one tutoring should assign trained staff rather than volunteers.
requirements: Access to classroom teachers, reading teachers, or well-prepared paraprofessionals to serve as tutors
constraints: Community volunteers are not suggested as tutors
target_learners: first-grade struggling readers
target_learning_goals: improved word attack and passage comprehension
examples: In the evaluated model, tutors may be the child's own teacher, a Title I teacher, or a part-time teacher added to the staff
key_sources: Early Steps. (2024). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/early-steps/

article_title: Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models
citation: Alice Xu, Icy (Yunyi) Zhang, Adam B. Blake and James W. Stigler. (2026). Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9099
title: Triangulate trace data with other sources to strengthen validity of inferences about learning
description: Because trace logs capture what learners do but not the underlying cognitive or metacognitive processes, the article advises that "To strengthen the validity of inferences drawn from trace data, it is important to triangulate with other data sources that offer more direct insight into learners' thinking". Modelable systems should combine trace data with embedded assessments and self-report measures so aligned sources collectively enhance inferential validity.
requirements: Additional data sources offering direct insight into learners' thinking, such as embedded assessments and self-report surveys, must be collected alongside trace data.
constraints: Logging behavior alone is not sufficient, as it captures only what learners do, not the processes underlying those actions.
target_learners: learners interacting with digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of engagement, cognition, and metacognition for learning analytics
examples: CourseKata triangulates enGauge trace data with over 1,500 embedded formative assessments and multi-point self-report surveys on motivation and interest.
key_sources: Alice Xu, Icy (Yunyi) Zhang, Adam B. Blake and James W. Stigler. (2026). Modelability as a Strategy for Improving the Generalizability and Scalability of Predictive Models. Journal of Learning Analytics, 13(1). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2026.9099

article_title: Changes in Math Instruction and Student Outcomes since the Implementation of Common Core State Standards in Chicago
citation: Julia A. Gwynne and Sarah Cashdollar. (2018). Changes in Math Instruction and Student Outcomes since the Implementation of Common Core State Standards in Chicago. UChicago Consortium working paper. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/
title: Three-tier train-the-trainer professional development cascade through school networks
description: A district-scale professional development delivery pattern in which each school network sends experienced teachers to full-day district-sponsored sessions three to four times per year; these teacher facilitators "replicated these sessions at network Teacher Leader Institutes," and teacher leaders then share the content with colleagues in their own schools. The district considered this three-tier distributed approach the best way to reach its sizeable workforce. The pattern trades reach for control: the district had less assurance that every teacher received the professional development, and participation levels varied widely across schools.
requirements: Organized school networks with identified experienced teacher facilitators and time for Teacher Leader Institutes
Coordination of session content across years
constraints: The district had less control over making sure each and every teacher received professional development on the new standards
target_learners: All district math teachers, network leaders, and administrators
target_learning_goals: Building capacity to teach to new, more challenging standards
examples: CPS delivered CCSS-M professional learning through network facilitators attending district sessions, network Teacher Leader Institutes, and school-level sharing
key_sources: Julia A. Gwynne and Sarah Cashdollar. (2018). Changes in Math Instruction and Student Outcomes since the Implementation of Common Core State Standards in Chicago. article_title: Educational Technology
citation: Holly M. Hart, Elaine Allensworth, Douglas L. Lauen, Robert M. Gladden. (2002). Educational Technology: Availability and Use in Chicago's Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Transparent technology use embedded in authentic project tasks
description: The article presents a lesson-level pattern in which technology serves an instructional goal naturally rather than as an add-on: in a collaborative recycling project, student groups use digital cameras for peer interviews, produce educational videos, survey classrooms and analyze data into graphs and charts, and design a web page. The authors call this "transparent technology use" that services the instruction goal "in a way that is natural and endemic rather than being an awkward addition to an old task."
requirements: Sufficient access to the needed devices and software for multiple concurrent student groups
target_learners: Elementary and secondary students in project-based classrooms
target_learning_goals: Data collection and analysis, communication of findings, and collaborative inquiry
examples: Two teachers collaborated on a recycling project in which four student groups used cameras, video production, survey data analysis, and web page design

article_title: MAP Growth Spanish Technical Report- Addendum
citation: MAP Growth Technical Report Spanish Addendum for 2024–2025. (2026). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Transadaptation of calibrated English items into culturally and linguistically appropriate Spanish items
description: A structured item-development process in which "The Spanish Math item bank is composed entirely of items that have been transadapted using a careful and highly structured process that starts with calibrated English Math items." Items are adaptations, not only translations: original English content is adapted for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, guided by International Test Commission guidelines, with glossaries, linguistic and content editing, proofreading in generic neutral Spanish for U.S. Spanish speakers, and expert validation that the Spanish item preserves the original construct and quality.
requirements: Selection of English source items with strong content and alignment that are culturally neutral or have adaptable parallel terms
Review stages covering linguistic editing, content editing, and proofreading, followed by subject-matter expert validation and a final quality check
constraints: Some English items are removed from development rather than translated when context or linguistic complexity makes them non-viable candidates
target_learners: Spanish-speaking students in U.S. K–12 assessments
target_learning_goals: Measuring the same mathematical constructs across languages
Preserving item construct and skill targeting when moving between English and Spanish
examples: Each Spanish Math item keeps the same standards alignment as its English counterpart and adopts the same RIT value; Wang and Li (2020) found English- and Spanish-calibrated item parameters were similar enough that separate calibrations were not required
key_sources: MAP Growth Technical Report Spanish Addendum for 2024–2025. (2026). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/map-growth-spanish-technical-report-addendum/

article_title: Mitigating the Academic Impacts of Proximity to Homicide: The Role of Schools
citation: Johnson, D.W., Hinze-Pifer, R., Orta, D., & Guz, S. (2024). Mitigating the academic impacts of proximity to homicide: The role of schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Build trusting educator-student relationships and broadly restorative responses to misconduct to protect students from adversity
description: The report holds that the particular quality of relationships between educators and students is a critically important barometer of success in mitigating the impacts of proximity to homicide. It states that "Efforts to make school systems and structures—particularly how a school responds to student misconduct—broadly restorative are an important part of the broader strategy of focusing on relationship and connectedness." Interviews in mitigating schools highlighted communication, coordination, and trust across the school community.
requirements: Sustained effort building collaborative, trusting relationships among adults in the school
School leaders who help create and sustain responsive school communities
constraints: Responsive, resilient school communities do not emerge from a single initiative and require substantial resources and sustained hard work
target_learners: Students exposed to community violence, particularly students of color in high-poverty communities
target_learning_goals: Academic performance, engagement, and resilience in the aftermath of adverse experiences
examples: Mitigating schools emphasized trusting, connected relationships among students and between students and adults across a range of climate measures

article_title: Spanish MAP Growth Reading technical report
citation: NWEA. (2021). Spanish MAP Growth Reading Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Transadaptation: adapting English assessment items into culturally and linguistically appropriate Spanish rather than translating them
description: The transadaptation process converts selected English assessment items into Spanish versions that are not translations but adaptations. The report states "The Spanish items are not translations but rather transadaptations of the English items. Original English content was adapted to be culturally and linguistically appropriate in Spanish." Experts consider regionalisms and dialects, cultural differences, grammatical features, and content appropriateness, guided by International Test Commission guidelines, followed by linguistic editing, content editing, and proofreading rounds.
requirements: Subject matter experts and content specialists review candidate items for cultural neutrality or appropriate parallel terms and concepts
Glossaries, style guides, and terminology are compiled for consistency, and items undergo three rounds of review (linguistic editing, content editing, proofreading)
constraints: Some English items are rejected as untranslatable; items with copyright or public domain passages were excluded from transadaptation
target_learners: Spanish-speaking students in United States schools taking Spanish-language reading assessments
target_learning_goals: Parallel measurement of reading skills across English and Spanish language arts constructs
examples: About 1,350 items were transadapted from the English pool, while about 2,250 native Spanish items were developed across Grades K–8 to cover Spanish-only standards such as accents and sound-symbol correspondence

article_title: Designing a Process for Micro-credentials at Scale
citation: Michelle Riconscente, Designs for Learning, Inc. (2016). Designing a Process for Micro-credentials at Scale. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Make micro-credential review processes transparent and consistent to build stakeholder trust and credibility
description: The article argues that describing a common process and providing transparency into how micro-credentials are scored and reviewers are certified is key to gaining the trust of educators, districts, states, and recognizing organizations. It states that putting in place transparent and consistent review processes can contribute to the trust-building and credibility essential for long-term effectiveness of a micro-credentialing approach to professional learning.
requirements: A common process described publicly
Clearly describing the validation approach taken, drawn when possible from a common set of options
target_learners: educators who would earn micro-credentials
districts, states and organizations who will recognize them
target_learning_goals: credible certification of educator competencies
examples: The article recommends issuers clearly describe the validation approach taken so those considering earning or recognizing the micro-credential are better informed

article_title: Year Up
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, November). Year Up. https://whatworks.ed.gov.
title: Combine occupational training with an employer internship and layered supports to improve early career earnings for disadvantaged young adults
description: The reviewed evidence indicates that a program model pairing full-time technical training with a subsequent employer internship, wrapped in advising, mentoring, stipends, and post-program placement services, can substantially raise short-term earnings for low-income young adults. The WWC judged this combination likely to increase short-term earnings, with an improvement index of +28 percentile points across two randomized trials. The model embeds work-based learning directly into occupational instruction and connects participants to employers in their target occupational fields.
requirements: Six months of full-time occupational and technical training aligned to employer needs
A six-month internship placement in the student's selected occupational field
Ongoing supports including advising, mentoring, and financial assistance throughout the program
constraints: The earnings advantage was demonstrated on short-term outcomes; medium-term earnings and employment showed no discernible effects, so the model's sustained impact beyond one year is not established by this evidence
Implementation depends on employer payments for interns, foundation grants, and charitable donations, which financed nearly all operating costs
target_learners: Low-income young adults ages 18 to 24 with a high school diploma or equivalent
target_learning_goals: Occupational and technical skills for entry-level positions in information technology and financial services
Professionalism and workplace behavior skills
Career planning, job search, and placement
examples: Year Up enrolled students in learning communities of about 40, delivered full-time training four and a half days a week for six months, then placed students in six-month internships with local companies in their selected occupational fields
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021, November). Year Up. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/722.

article_title: Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies
citation: Roschelle, J., Ruiz, P., Means, B., Griffiths, R., Lee, K. (2026 April). Towards an Evidence Framework for Emerging Educational Technologies. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/289
title: Trails Up a Mountain: stakeholder-specific evidence paths toward a shared peak
description: Trails Up a Mountain is a workshop visualization depicting 'different paths along a journey (or climb) to related destinations', recognizing that technology developers, school procurement leaders, and researchers each use evidence in different ways at different times. Unlike a strict tier ladder, it preserves the idea of a desirable peak of evidence that all perspectives are climbing towards, while allowing evidence journeys to intersect at key moments or conversations.

constraints: The article notes researchers and practitioners often operate under different evidentiary standards, illustrated by disagreement over simulated-student evidence
target_learners: School procurement leaders
technology developers
researchers
target_learning_goals: Aligning evidence generation and use across stakeholder roles
examples: School leaders might start by finding out what is working at schools like mine, while developers might start from proof of concept of a learning-process improvement

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework
citation: Graciela N. Borsato, Jenny Nagaoka, and Ellen Foley. (2013). College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework. Voices in Urban Education, Fall 2013. https://vue.annenberginstitute.org
title: Tri-level approach: indicators at individual, setting, and system levels
description: The CRIS framework posits that solely considering student-level outcome indicators does not suffice; context must be monitored to see whether conditions for college readiness are in place. Individual-level indicators measure students' personal progress; setting-level indicators track school resources and opportunities such as college-going culture and AP availability; system-level indicators focus on district policy and funding infrastructure such as guidance counselors, professional development, and data resources. The three dimensions combined with the three levels form a 3 x 3 matrix called the CRIS Menu.
requirements: A comprehensive indicator system must include indicators at all three levels, not only the individual level
target_learners: high school students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: monitoring conditions that promote college readiness
examples: System-level indicators signal the extent to which district-level resources are in place to carry out an effective college readiness agenda

article_title: California's English Learners and Their Long-Term Learning Outcomes
citation: Novicoff, S., Reardon, S. F., & Johnson, R. C. (2024). California's English learners and their long-term learning outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/636.224
title: Track English learners as kindergarten-entry cohorts over time rather than as a point-in-time snapshot to avoid selection bias from reclassification
description: The report argues that studying only current ELs distorts the picture of EL progress, because the highest-achieving ELs are reclassified out of the EL pool and newcomers enter it later. It instead follows "all California public school students who began receiving EL services starting in kindergarten" through all subsequent years, including years after reclassification. The authors state that "We can more clearly gauge the progress of EL students using this longitudinal, tracking-over-years approach."
requirements: Longitudinal student-level administrative data linking EL status, demographics, and test scores across years
constraints: Excludes students who enter the school system after kindergarten, such as newcomers; cannot track students who move out of state
target_learners: English learners in K–12 public schools
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency acquisition
academic achievement in ELA and math
examples: The report shows the traditional snapshot view (Figure 2) yields a widening gap, while the K-cohort framework (Figure 3) reveals shrinking gaps for the same students

article_title: Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars
citation: Pascal Riachi, Sofie Kamber, Stella Brogna, Andrew Gloster, Rafael Wampfler. (2026). Toward Accessible Psychotherapy Training Using AI-Driven Interactive Patient Avatars. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17786
title: Transcript-derived patient profiles conditioning virtual patient behavior across seven dimensions
description: Four anonymized patient profiles (two male, two female) were synthesized with GPT-5.2 from 4–7 real ACT sessions each, which "averaged 58–92 therapist-patient turn pairs and lasted 38–60 minutes". A structured prompt extracted stable patterns across seven dimensions (patient overview, core difficulties, values and motivations, emotional and cognitive themes, behavioral patterns, progress trajectory, simulation hooks) and constrained the model to rely only on transcript content and produce anonymized descriptions.
requirements: Real therapy transcripts as source material
Joint analysis of multiple sessions to capture stable patterns
constraints: Profiles are anonymized approximations derived only from transcript content
target_learners: Psychotherapists in training
target_learning_goals: Clinically plausible patient interaction practice
examples: Suicidal ideation scenarios are paired only with profiles characterized by burnout and shame, not with profiles centered on interpersonal conflict without depressive features.

article_title: Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education
citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Trustworthiness serves as a structured lens for evaluating LLMs in education, bridging abstract ethical principles and operational technical requirements
description: The article proposes adapting trustworthiness criteria from the ML community as a structured lens for LLM evaluation in education. Trustworthiness functions as an anchor that connects high-level ethical concerns (fairness, safety) to concrete, quantifiable measurements that learning engineers can apply per response. The authors argue this lens helps "bridge the LLM evaluation gap" by providing measurements that help learning engineers align on education-specific challenges and systematically identify potential pedagogical disruptions before deployment.
requirements: Trustworthiness dimensions must be adapted and re-contextualized to the educational deployment context, since which dimensions matter is a property of the deployment
constraints: Ethical frameworks describe principles rather than measurements, leaving open how a learning engineer should check a specific response before it reaches a learner
target_learners: learning engineers
educational technology developers
target_learning_goals: evaluating LLM responses for pedagogical alignment
identifying pedagogical disruptions before deployment
examples: The authors adapted Huang et al.'s eight dimensions of trustworthy LLMs as a starting framework, then filtered and adjusted measures through co-design sessions with learning engineers
key_sources: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006

article_title: Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education
citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Six visualizations for tracing and comparing trustworthiness metric violations across LLM responses
description: The article co-designed six visualizations that help learning engineers trace where each trustworthiness metric was violated in an LLM response and compare relative performance across multiple responses. Key design features include "Highlighting violations in LLM response" and "Explanations for metric violations." Visualizations map each violation onto the span of the response, the learner's message, or the passage responsible, enabling raters to verify flags against the source text before acting on them.
requirements: Visualizations should show which metrics each response violates and where two responses differ before a rater reads either one closely
Each violation must be traceable to the specific text span responsible
constraints: Visualization literacy of collaborators was a design consideration, requiring simpler views that avoid complex analytical thought
target_learners: learning engineers evaluating LLM responses
target_learning_goals: calibrating expert judgment of LLM trustworthiness
supporting A/B comparison of LLM responses
examples: A rater who sees a hallucination flagged should be able to jump straight to the sentence that caused it

article_title: From fear to innovation: A case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education
citation: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x
title: Faculty development for AI integration should be transformative and equity-oriented rather than compliance-based tool training
description: The article argues that faculty development for AI must move beyond compliance-based training focused on detection or technical tools toward reflective, equity-oriented, future-facing engagement. It states this "requires more than technical training; it demands fundamental reconsideration of pedagogical philosophies, assessment strategies, and the very purposes of higher education in an AI-augmented world". The UBRIDGE institute operationalized this principle.
requirements: Development must acknowledge and engage faculty's fundamental philosophical concerns (preservationist, innovator, pragmatist perspectives) rather than treating AI integration as merely a technical challenge
constraints: The authors note institutional barriers persist around policy clarity, institutional support structures, and AI's perceived legitimacy
target_learners: Higher education faculty across the adoption spectrum, including skeptics
target_learning_goals: Ethical reasoning about AI use
Pedagogical transformation for AI-augmented teaching
examples: The institute paired hands-on experimentation in a supportive environment with structured experiences that acknowledged concerns, which the authors credit for the fear-to-curiosity shift

article_title: E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement
citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: Tripartite framework of engagement: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions
description: The article adopts the tripartite framework from educational psychology, which identifies "three interconnected aspects of engagement: behavioral participation and attention, emotional interest and enjoyment, and cognitive effort and depth of processing". The framework motivates E3Sense's measurement design and frames the qualitative analysis: learners' own interview definitions of engagement were found to align with these dimensions while showing that different learners emphasize different criteria when giving the same overall rating.
requirements: Used to motivate the system and discuss learners' accounts, while targeting a single overall self-reported engagement rating as the prediction outcome
constraints: The dimensions are related but dissociable, and none of the physiological channels provides a unique reading of one engagement dimension
target_learners: video-based learners whose engagement is being sensed
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing engagement as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions to guide measurement and personalized interpretation
examples: Exit-interview quotes illustrate each dimension: cognitive (learning something new), behavioral (not zoning out), and emotional (interest and curiosity)
key_sources: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569

article_title: Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS)
citation: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936
title: GenAI systems should build trust by being transparent about process, purpose, and performance
description: A workshop roundtable principle of good GenAI design holds that "GenAI systems should build trust by being more transparent aboutprocess, purpose, and performance". Regarding process, systems should explain how an answer or output was generated, including which sources informed it; regarding purpose, systems should elicit the user's higher-level purpose to provide appropriate support; regarding performance, systems should convey their level of confidence about the accuracy and completeness of a response. The workshop also called for methodologies to measure the extent to which systems exhibit these principles.
requirements: methodologies to measure the extent to which systems exhibit principles of good GenAI design
target_learners: academic search system users, including researchers and students
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and responsible use of GenAI-mediated academic search
examples: the Foundations & Principles roundtable elaborated process, purpose, and performance transparency with concrete examples such as revealing which sources informed an output

article_title: Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks
citation: Yubo Li, Rema Padman, Ramayya Krishnan. (2026). Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22606
title: TransplantQA corpus: 102 US transplant handbooks from 23 centers paired with 1,115 patient-derived questions
description: TransplantQA is a benchmark pairing institutional patient-education handbooks with patient-derived questions for auditing retrieval-augmented patient-facing AI. The article states "The TransplantQA corpus contains 102 patient-education handbooks from 23 U.S. solid-organ transplant centers, covering 16 of the 20 largest U.S. programs by procedure volume." Questions were curated from public institutional Q&A pages, community forums, and patient-facing medical organizations, filtered from over 3,000 candidates, and labelled with organ and a 13-topic taxonomy.

citation: Zhiqi Gao, Huarui Luo, Guo Zhu, Bingquan Zhang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Yizhan Feng, Jiahuan Pei, Jie Li, Benyou Wang. (2026). MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17512

description: MedEasy's post-session evaluation compares the retained consultation trajectory — dialogue history, recognized intents, elicited facts, clinical actions, decisions, and medical-record entries — with an expert-authored reference answer. "The evaluation follows six modules: history taking, physical examination, auxiliary examination, diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, and overall performance." article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Make the literacy demands of each entanglement type explicit to students (transparency)
description: The first design principle the review derives is transparency: "teachers could make the literacy demands of each type of entanglement explicit to students." For Assistant and Enabler activities, where demands largely cohere across levels, this means clarifying what individual competence means in GenAI-supported work, including where the boundary lies between legitimate use and overreliance. For Generator, Reimaginator, and Synthesizer activities, where demands are more fractured, it means naming the tension directly — for example, that Reimaginator students take epistemic responsibility for outputs they did not conventionally produce while being evaluated as if individually authored.
requirements: Teachers must clarify how epistemic work may be distributed between students and GenAI, what counts as legitimate participation, and how the activity relates to institutional expectations
constraints: The appropriate form of transparency differs by entanglement type: clarifying boundaries for coherent types versus naming tensions directly for fractured types
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: identifying tensions embedded in GenAI activities and responding to them productively rather than experiencing them as confusion
examples: In Reimaginator entanglement, teachers clarify that students are asked to take epistemic responsibility for outputs they did not produce in a conventional sense while still being evaluated as if the work were individually authored

citation: Singh, N. P., Wang, X., Garikipati, A., Ciobanu, M., Mao, Q., & Das, R. (2026). Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised Fine-Tuning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06385
title: Target LLM training on the model's own failure modes with progressive difficulty and difficulty-weighted sampling
description: The article's training strategy identifies the base model's weaknesses empirically and concentrates learning capacity there. The base model was tested with 30 attempts per question; questions answered correctly in all attempts were excluded, and the remainder were sorted by error frequency into a difficulty-ordered curriculum. In SFT, questions with high baseline accuracy contributed a single representative example while difficult questions retained all high-quality examples, with increased training weights on high-difficulty items. The authors report this "difficulty-aware training strategy helped address the typical performance degradation that models experience on complex edge cases."

constraints: Demonstrated on teacher-exam-style multiple-choice questions; the article notes future work should examine free-form tutoring dialogs

target_learning_goals: pedagogical knowledge, particularly performance on challenging pedagogical scenarios

article_title: Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction
citation: Lixiang Yan, Yueqiao Jin, Xibin Han, Dragan Gasevic. (2026). Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23426
title: Truth-default theory extended to presumed human identity in computer-mediated interaction
description: The article applies truth-default theory — the account that in ordinary interaction people default to presuming honesty and benign intent unless contextual triggers raise suspicion — to presumed human identity in synchronous text-based interaction. It argues that socially fluent AI "effectively decoupled social signaling from source identity, rendering established computer-mediated communication heuristics non-diagnostic". The theory explains why participants exhibited a slight bias toward human attribution and why suspicion cues such as perceived scriptedness or rapid response can be shared by both AI and human targets.
requirements: Undisclosed interaction under truth-default conditions, where suspicion is not externally prompted
constraints: Findings bounded to undisclosed, synchronous, text-based group interaction; identity inference may differ with richer modalities or explicit warnings that AI may be present
target_learners: adult online collaborators
target_learning_goals: inferring interlocutor identity and intent from conversational cues in online interaction

article_title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Trust calibration account: users adjust reliance on robots according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected competence rather than appearance
description: The article explains its findings through trust calibration theories from automation research. On this account, users calibrate trust to contextual demands: "users adjust their reliance on artificial agents according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected system competence rather than agent appearance alone". Instructional tasks are structured, goal-oriented, and objectively verifiable, reducing uncertainty and promoting confidence, whereas personal conversations involving emotional disclosure introduce higher social and privacy sensitivity, leading users to apply stricter trust criteria.
requirements: Applies to interactions where users can perceive task risk and expected agent competence, such as structured instruction versus personal disclosure
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of this study's video-based results, consistent with cited contextual-factor findings; not directly tested as a mechanism in the experiment
target_learners: undergraduate future educators
target_learning_goals: calibration of trust in socially assistive robots across educational task contexts
examples: The article links the T2 > T1 > T3 trust ordering to lower perceived risk in verifiable instructional tasks and higher privacy sensitivity in personal-information discussions

article_title: How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study
citation: Fu L, Ouyang Z and Wu Q (2026). How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study. Front. Psychol. 17:1900061. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900061
title: Temporally ordered trust→fairness→motivation model for AI teaching assistants with three within-person mechanisms
description: The article proposes a temporally ordered model in which trust functions as an antecedent cognitive-affective orientation associated with subsequent within-person change in fairness evaluations, which in turn influence motivational outcomes. It rests on three mechanisms: an attributional schema mechanism, a cognitive load mechanism, and a justice-emotion mechanism. As the article states, "trust creates attributional schemas that filter fairness evaluations: high-trust individuals interpret ambiguous system behaviors charitably, attributing apparent inconsistencies to benign causes, whereas low-trust individuals engage in vigilant monitoring for injustice evidence". The model integrates trust theory, organizational justice theory, and self-determination theory, and was tested with RI-CLPM longitudinal mediation.
requirements: Three-wave (or longer) longitudinal measurement with intervals matched to the theorized timescale of trust–fairness recalibration
Random-intercept decomposition to separate stable between-person trait variance from within-person fluctuation
constraints: The article notes cross-sectional designs cannot separate stable between-person differences from genuine within-person change, motivating the longitudinal specification
Benevolence trust may function differently for non-sentient AI than in interpersonal trust contexts, as the article acknowledges
target_learners: undergraduate students using AI teaching assistants in higher education
target_learning_goals: sustained learning motivation toward AI-mediated instruction
examples: The study tested the model with a three-wave RI-CLPM (N = 450, 4-week intervals) including longitudinal mediation via bias-corrected bootstrapping

The article uses it not to compare perspectives but as a process in which "student dialogue as evidence" progressively refines educators' interpretations across three stages: initial educator dialogue, student dialogue, and educator reflective reconstruction. It positions the method as narrowing the gap between observable programming products and actual AI-supported learning processes.

undergraduate computer science students

article_title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model (TRACE)
citation: Paul Savala. (2026). Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13409
title: TRACE: a Transformer architecture with semester-level concurrency encoding and joint course-set/grade prediction
description: TRACE (a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation) encodes a student's major, course and grade history with separate embedding layers and positional encodings based on relative semester, so all courses in the same semester share a temporal vector, enforcing a permutation-invariant representation within each term while preserving order across terms. Its decoder jointly predicts the next semester's course set and grades, trained with a novel loss combining KL divergence over the course distribution and MSE for grade regression. The author states this "enforces a permutation-invariant representation within each semester, which we argue more accurately reflects the unordered nature of concurrent enrollments."
requirements: Requires historical enrollment, grade and major data from which course and major embeddings are learned without hand-encoded features
A weighting factor ω balancing the two loss terms should be optimized via cross-validation; the author found a value near one was optimal
constraints: New courses outside the training vocabulary map to an <OTHER> token, limiting prediction for novel curricula
A cold-start problem exists for new students with no academic history
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: predicting next-semester course enrollment and grade performance for early alert and advising
examples: Trained on 5326 students, 360 courses, 48 majors and 18 semesters (Fall 2014 through Fall 2023) from a single American university, with 90/10 train-test split

article_title: A Critical Narrative Synthesis of Psychological Correlates, Measurement, and Reported Findings on Conversational AI Engagement and Dependence-Related Constructs
citation: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795
title: Construct-boundary taxonomy distinguishing trust, reliance, over-reliance, attachment/companionship, and dysregulated dependence
description: The review argues the literature treats trust, reliance, over-reliance, attachment, companionship, problematic use, and dependence as one continuum when they are non-equivalent constructs. Trust concerns expectations about system competence; reliance is the behavioral decision to delegate; over-reliance is delegation without adequate scrutiny; attachment and companionship concern emotional closeness; and "Dysregulated dependence and problematic use require stronger evidence of impaired control, compulsive return, withdrawal-like discomfort, or negative impact." Conversational-AI engagement serves as the broad, non-pathologizing umbrella term.
requirements: Dependence labeling requires evidence of impaired control or functional harm, not merely frequent use, reliance, or attachment
constraints: The taxonomy is an interpretive organization of the corpus, not a validated latent structure
target_learners: Researchers, instrument developers, and educators interpreting AI-use measures
target_learning_goals: Construct separation and design-matched claims about AI engagement and dependence

article_title: A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education
citation: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026
title: Tripartite feedback framework: three feedback levels distinguished by epistemic status for human-AI task allocation
description: The framework distinguishes three analytically distinct feedback levels: low-level structural and presentational feedback, intermediate-level factual content validation, and high-level critical evaluation and synthesis. It categorizes feedback by epistemic status — "rule-based/factual verification/interpretive evaluation" — to provide "a basis for human–technology decisions". The levels are "distinct dimensions, not a hierarchy", and the framework complements rather than replaces Hattie and Timperley's learning-level model.

critical evaluation and disciplinary reasoning

citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: Constrain or truncate stochastic approximation iterates rather than allowing unbounded iterates
description: The book advocates constrained algorithms in which iterates that leave a prescribed set are projected back into it. When a parameter takes excessive values, "one would normally alter the unconstrained algorithm if the parameter θ took on excessive values. The simplest alteration is truncation." The authors argue that "allowing unbounded iterates seems to be of greater mathematical than practical interest," because model physics at large parameter values are often poorly known. Practical algorithms should also include other safeguards against bad noise or inappropriate step sizes.

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Cognitive load / transience account: segmentation reduces extraneous load from information transience by dividing content into smaller units and providing processing pauses
description: This account, grounded in cognitive load theory and the time-based resource-sharing model of working memory, explains why transient dynamic visualizations can hinder learning: information is continuously replaced, so learners must maintain earlier information in working memory while processing new incoming information. Segmentation addresses this because "pauses between segments provide students with sufficient time to attend to necessary cognitive activities on the bit of information presented in the previous segment, without having to simultaneously attend to new incoming information." The review attributes the effectiveness of segmentation partly to this reduction of the co-occurrence of processing activities.
requirements: Applies to complex dynamic visualizations that are high in intrinsic load, where extraneous load must be decreased so learning is not hampered
constraints: Providing pauses increases total available learning time, but the review argues the effect is not simply due to learning time, citing Hasler et al. (2007) where learning time was equal across conditions
target_learners: Students learning from complex dynamic visualizations, especially novices
target_learning_goals: Understanding of processes and procedures depicted in animations and videos
examples: The review interprets the segmented-condition advantages in the Mayer and Chandler (2001), Moreno (2007), and Hasler et al. (2007) studies through this load-reduction mechanism

article_title: Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?
citation: Bouzidi, L., & Jaillet, A. (2009). Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?. Educational Technology & Society, 12(4), 257-268. https://www.ifets.info/
title: Trust peer assessment only for exact-science exams marked by at least four peers with quality precautions in place
description: The article recommends accepting peer assessment as valid when exams contain exact-science questions (calculations, mathematical reasoning, short algorithms, short texts) and each paper is marked by at least four peers, supported by safeguards. Anonymity and providing exam solutions to assessors are among the recommended supports.

article_title: Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond
citation: Na'ilah Suad Nasir, Victoria Hand and Edd V. Taylor. (2008). Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond. Review of Research in Education, Vol. 32. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X07308962
title: Tripartite analytic framework of culture in mathematics learning: knowing, learning, and the educational system as cultural
description: The chapter proposes an analytic framework locating the boundary between cultural and domain mathematics knowledge at three levels of social activity: mathematics knowing as a cultural activity (everyday vs. school math structures and discourse), mathematics learning as a cultural enterprise (classroom vs. home and local community), and mathematics education as a cultural system (access to and positioning in the field). The authors state the levels are "analytically distinct" yet "reflexively related," and they shift gaze between levels to capture how researchers perceive culture-math relations. The framework organizes the chapter's literature synthesis.
requirements: Research questions must specify which level of social activity — knowing, learning, or the system — is being analyzed
constraints: The authors treat the three levels as analytically distinct for the chapter's purposes while recognizing they constitute each other
target_learners: nondominant and marginalized students in American schools, particularly students from groups underperforming in mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematical knowing and reasoning
equitable access to opportunities to learn rich mathematics
examples: The basketball players' study illustrates the first level: practice-linked knowing inaccessible in the math classroom
NCLB policy debates illustrate the third level, the cultural system of mathematics education

article_title: Role of linguistic skills in fifth-grade mathematics
citation: Kleemans, T., Segers, E., & Verhoeven, L. (2018). Role of linguistic skills in fifth-grade mathematics. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 167, 404-413. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2017.11.012

The authors propose that the results "hint at an extension of the verbal system of the triple code model" by including both phonological skills and grammatical ability as key variables of exact arithmetic calculations, and note that grammatical ability and arithmetic share underlying rules and recursive principles.

Geometry
Fractions

article_title: The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children
citation: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/
title: Target inhibition training as a potential shared component influencing EF, WM, and intelligence in young children
description: The article's practical implication is that inhibition, shown to correlate with both intelligence and verbal WM in kindergartners, may be the most efficient training target. The authors state: "it may be promising to target training inhibition as a potential shared component between EF, WM, and intelligence to have an influence on all three constructs." This rests on their finding that inhibition accuracy correlated with intelligence even after partialling out verbal WM, while the reverse did not hold.
requirements: Interventions should target the inhibition component specifically, as the evidence base for inhibition as the shared component comes from correlational findings in kindergarten-age children.
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational evidence in 5.5- to 7.5-year-olds, not on a training experiment in this study; the authors note EF training transfer appears to be narrow (Diamond and Ling 2016).
target_learners: Kindergarten children (ages 5.5–7.5)
target_learning_goals: Executive function development, particularly inhibitory control
examples: The study measured inhibition via accuracy in the incongruent block of the Hearts and Flowers task, where children had to press the button opposite to the flower's side, inhibiting a prepotent response established in the congruent hearts block.

article_title: Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults
citation: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294
title: Triple-Code-Model of number processing and calculation
description: The Triple-Code-Model (TCM) holds that numerical information is processed by three distinct representational codes supported by regionally and functionally distinct neural substrates: an analogue magnitude representation mediating approximate and discrete quantity processing, a visual Arabic number form supporting recognition of Arabic numerals, and an auditory verbal word frame used for verbally mediated operations and direct arithmetic fact retrieval. The review states the TCM "has shaped decades of numerical cognition research" in healthy adults, patients, and developmental studies, though it may not directly apply to developing brain systems.
requirements: Developed from adult data and mature brain systems; the review notes it might not be directly applicable to developmental brain systems
constraints: Based on adult data, so applicability to developmental populations is limited per the review

adults with developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: number processing and calculation
arithmetic fact retrieval
numerical magnitude representation

citation: Portilla Ximena A., Ballard Parissa J., Adler Nancy E., Boyce W. Thomas, Obradović Jelena. (2014). An Integrative View of School Functioning: Transactions between Self-Regulation, School Engagement, and Teacher-Child Relationship Quality. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12259
title: Transactional model of development applied to early schooling: children's behaviors and teacher-child relationship quality shape each other bidirectionally over time
description: Extending Sameroff and MacKenzie's (2003) transactional model to a school context, the article theorizes that children's behaviors and the classroom environment, indexed by teacher-child relationship quality, "interact through bidirectional processes" over time, forming patterns that serve as both inputs and outcomes to development. article_title: The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving.
citation: Thevenot, C., Dewi, J., Bagnoud, J., Wolfer, P., Fayol, M., & Castel, C. (2018). The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Train counting procedures through intensive practice before old age rather than overemphasizing rote memorization of arithmetic facts
description: The article argues that because arithmetic expertise in addition is "most likely to be achieved through procedural automatization than retrieval of the answers from long-term memory", overemphasizing rote memorization during learning "may be misguided". Instead, "repeated use of a procedure as counting might be more efficient than memorization of direct associations between operands and answers". Because intensive practice in old age does not yield the performance levels reached by younger adults, the authors conclude that "training programs take place before the cognitive system departs excessively from its optimum level of efficiency".
requirements: Intensive, repeated practice of counting procedures, administered before the cognitive system departs excessively from its optimum level of efficiency.
constraints: Intensive practice in old age does not bring the same level of performance as that reached by younger adults (citing Maquestiaux et al., 2013; Touron et al., 2001).
target_learners: primary school children
adults of new generations
adults who do not age so successfully
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fluency
automatization of counting procedures
preservation of arithmetic abilities into old age
examples: The article cites Tournaki (2003) showing that an intervention based on repetitive counting-on from the largest addend (3 + 4 = 5, 6, 7) is more efficient to develop arithmetic skills than a drill-and-practice training program.

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x

description: The authors invoke the triangle model of reading development (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004; Plaut et al., 1996) to explain why expressive vocabulary relates to exception word reading. In this model, "vocabulary knowledge is connected to word reading knowledge and, therefore, individual differences in vocabulary knowledge are related to individual variability in word reading knowledge." Simulation studies cited by the authors show words with inconsistent phonological mappings rely more on semantic information than words with consistent mappings, accounting for the vocabulary–exception-word link.

constraints: The article offers the model as an interpretive framework for correlational findings; it did not test the model directly.

Reading comprehension

article_title: Learning motivation mediates gene-by-socioeconomic status interaction on mathematics achievement in early childhood
citation: Tucker-Drob, Elliot M., & Harden, K. Paige. (2011). Learning Motivation Mediates Gene-by-Socioeconomic Status Interaction on Mathematics Achievement in Early Childhood. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2011.11.015
title: Transactional gene-environment interaction account: high-opportunity environments let children select, evoke, and attend to learning experiences congruent with genetically influenced motivation
description: The article advances a transactional developmental account (citing Dickens and Flynn, Scarr, and Tucker-Drob & Harden) in which heritable variation in achievement is expressed through child-driven processes. As the authors write, "heritable variation in cognition and achievement comes to be expressed through a process by which children select, evoke, and attend to experiences that are congruent with their genetically influenced traits." In high-opportunity environments children can match learning experiences to their genotypes, so achievement becomes increasingly heritable; in low-opportunity environments this matching is constrained and heritable variation stays low. The study's mediation results are presented as evidence for this mechanism operating via learning motivation in early childhood.
requirements: Adequate environmental opportunity for enriching interactions with the proximal environment, so that motivated children can translate non-cognitive traits into cognitive skills
constraints: The authors note that in low-opportunity environments children are less able to match their learning experiences to their genotypes, suppressing heritable variation in achievement
target_learners: four-year-old children (early childhood, prior to formal schooling)
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement and school readiness
examples: The bivariate twin analyses showed only the genetic pathway from motivation to achievement varied with SES, which the authors interpret as support for this transactional process

article_title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6
title: Transactivity as reasoning of one utterance building on another, analyzable at individual or group unit
description: Stahl defines transactivity as "the reasoning of one utterance building on another utterance's reasoning" and argues it can be analyzed two ways: as mental states of individuals A and B exchanging utterances P and Q, or as a group-level unity where meaning lies in the pair P-Q rather than in individual minds. article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Transactivity framework: other-oriented versus self-oriented transacts as operationalized building-on-reasoning moves
description: The article operationalizes transactivity as reasoning made explicit that builds on prior reasoning in a discussion. As printed, "our operationalization of transactivity is defined as the process of building on an idea expressed earlier in a conversation using a reasoning statement." Transacts are self-oriented when they operate on the speaker's own prior reasoning and other-oriented when they operate on a partner's reasoning; other-oriented transacts are treated as particularly central to group knowledge integration. article_title: How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning
citation: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7

description: The trigger regulation framework (Järvelä & Hadwin, 2024) conceptualizes regulation as initiated by identifiable trigger events rather than as a continuous background process. The article states that trigger events "act as metacognitive signals that indicate when some form of regulation is needed," reflecting cognitive, motivational, emotional, or behavioral challenges. It anchors regulation cycles in discrete challenge moments, enabling examination of when regulation begins, how monitoring unfolds, and how groups coordinate responses over time, and it was designed with multimodal SSRL research in mind, allowing trigger events to be identified across synchronized data channels. In this study it guided deductive video coding of challenges and regulation processes.
requirements: Trigger events must be identifiable as discrete challenge moments (cognitive, metacognitive, socioemotional, behavioral, motivational) across synchronized data channels
constraints: The framework explains challenges as metacognitive signals inviting regulation or adaptation, not as continuous background processes
target_learners: secondary school students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: socially shared regulation of learning during collaborative inquiry
examples: The framework guided deductive ELAN coding yielding eight codes, with inter-rater agreement of mean Cohen's kappa = 0.830 for challenges and 0.844 for regulation processes

article_title: “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education
citation: Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen, Päivi Häkkinen, Pasi Tarhonen, Piia Näykki, Sanna Järvelä. (2022). “Anything taking shape?” Capturing various layers of small group collaborative problem solving in an experiential geometry course in initial teacher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09562-5
title: Triangulating three analysis methods onto video data to capture various layers of CPS as a small-group enactment
description: The article develops a triangulated analysis method combining three equally valued approaches to understand CPS at group level: "(a) directed content analysis of the actualized CPS in groups, (b) process analysis and visualizations, and (c) qualitative cases". All analyses rest on video recordings of co-located group sessions. Content analysis provides cumulative frequency accounts, process analysis adds the temporal order and intensity of social and cognitive states, and qualitative cases return attention to micro-interaction processes. The authors argue this produces "a unified depiction in understanding CPS in this context" and divergent ways to understand CPS.

constraints: The article states the study scope does not cover how the pedagogical design affects the quality of CPS; the article notes cases "do not aim to generalize to populations"

target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving as a 21st-century skill; group-level CPS enactment during open-ended mathematics (geometry) tasks

citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Trace data from text highlighting and notes as an objective measure of cognitive strategy use
description: Trace data were gathered from participants' text highlighting and notes while learning a catastrophe-management text, with no instruction to highlight or take notes. The authors distinguish highlighted key words (nouns and explaining verbs and adverbs) from auxiliary words (pronouns, conjunctions, modal verbs), and notes were coded by two independent raters for cognitive learning strategies (ICC = 0.91). target_learning_goals: objective assessment of cognitive strategy use during text learning
examples: In the study, participants could use pens and highlighters by choice while preparing a text on catastrophe management, and their highlighting and notes were analyzed as trace data

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Triarchic theory of three kinds of cognitive processing during learning
description: Mayer's triarchic theory distinguishes three demands on the learner's limited cognitive capacity: "extraneous processing, which is cognitive processing that does not serve the instructional objective", "essential processing, which is cognitive processing required to mentally represent the presented material in working memory", and "generative processing, which is cognitive processing required to make sense of the material". Meaningful learning depends on selecting, organizing, and integrating material; the three kinds of processing map onto these processes in different degrees. Mayer offers it as a reconciliation of questions about the three kinds of cognitive load in cognitive load theory.
requirements: Instructional design should minimize extraneous processing while managing essential and fostering generative processing, per the theory's account
constraints: Mayer presents it as his own conceptualization within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, offered in hopes of reconciliation rather than as settled consensus
target_learners: multimedia learners in instructional settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning through appropriate cognitive processing of words and pictures
examples: Mayer reports the conceptualization helped discover several research-based principles of multimedia learning (Mayer 2009)

citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: Framework of triggers for iteration in instructional design
description: A framework listing concrete events that trigger iteration in instructional design, proposed because earlier reason-types were judged too coarse to predict when iteration should occur. Triggers 'originate from outside (new information, new opinions/arguments and acquisition procedures)' or are 'caused by, or evolve from interaction with the design process itself (discovery of missing input, need to repair errors, new insights based on work later on in the design process, and new ideas of the designers)'. It is intended as a basis for further research and for defining support measures for designers, especially novices.
requirements: Serves as a basis for further research and for the definition of measures that help designers, especially novices, deal with iteration during the design process.
constraints: Derived from one evaluation study with eight novice designers in the training-simulator domain; the article notes the limited number of subjects does not allow valid use of correlation coefficients.
target_learners: novice instructional designers
designers of training simulator specifications
target_learning_goals: managing iteration in the instructional design process
examples: In the study, scheduled design cycles and peer review most often provoked iteration, while a resources e-mail and chat sessions did so less often.

title: Triangular framework of dialogic feedback: cognitive, social-affective, and structural dimensions
description: The article draws on a triangular framework of the dialogic feedback process proposed by Yang and Carless (2013), in which "a triangular framework has been proposed that includes three dimensions: cognitive, social-affective, and structural". The cognitive dimension concerns feedback content that enhances students' cognitive abilities; the social-affective dimension underscores trust and balanced power relationships between educators and students; the structural dimension concerns management and organisation of the feedback process by educators and institutions. The study uses this framework, together with the learner-centred feedback framework, as a deductive coding lens for qualitative analysis of feedback design themes.
requirements: Feedback conceptualised as a reciprocal, dialogic process in which students take an active role in engaging with and responding to feedback, not a one-way transmission model.
constraints: The framework is attributed to Yang and Carless (2013); the article applies it as an analytical lens rather than testing it empirically.

target_learning_goals: engaging with and acting on feedback
self-regulated use of feedback
examples: The study's qualitative coding scheme grouped feedback design codes using this triangular framework alongside the learner-centred feedback framework (Ryan et al., 2022).

It affords multiple solution attempts, is part of the secondary school curriculum, and has been used in studies replicating the PF effect. The study paired it with a 45-minute instruction phase highlighting typical student errors against the canonical solution.

article_title: Improving the measurement of self-regulated learning using multi-channel data
citation: Yizhou Fan, Lyn Lim, Joep van der Graaf, Jonathan Kilgour, Mladen Raković, Johanna Moore, Inge Molenaar, Maria Bannert, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević. (2022). Improving the measurement of self-regulated learning using multi-channel data. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09304-z
title: Trace parser with action library and process library for measuring SRL from multi-channel data
description: A trace-based measurement protocol that converts raw multi-channel trace data into SRL processes. Its trace parser has two components: "the action library and the process library" — the action library labels raw log data with 12 learning actions, and the process library detects SRL processes from action sequences. The study examined "the eight groups of SRL processes: four groups of metacognitive and four groups of cognitive processes, including Orientation, Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation, First-reading, Re-reading, Elaborating and Organising", grounded in Bannert's (2007) theoretical framework and validated through theory-driven and data-driven perspectives.

A theoretical framework and coding scheme defining rules for identification of SRL processes

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: The trans-contextual model of autonomous motivation explains transfer of autonomous motivation from educational to out-of-school contexts
description: The trans-contextual model is a multitheory framework integrating self-determination theory, Vallerand's hierarchical model, and the theory of planned behavior to explain how motivation transfers across contexts. As the authors state, it "outlines the processes by which autonomous motivation toward activities in a physical education context predicts autonomous motivation toward physical activity outside of school, and beliefs about, intentions toward, and actual engagement in, out-of-school physical activity." The model comprises three propositions linking perceived autonomy support, autonomous motivation in educational contexts, autonomous motivation in out-of-school contexts, belief-based antecedents, intentions, and behavior.
requirements: Empirical support for the three model propositions and their fundamental hypotheses (H1-H5, H15) is required for the model to be accepted
constraints: Originally developed and predominantly tested in the physical education and leisure-time physical activity context, with generalizability to other domains proposed but not yet extensively tested

target_learning_goals: transfer of autonomous motivation from classroom activities to out-of-school engagement in related activities

citation: Jörg, T., Davis, B. & Nickmans, G. (2007). Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 145–156. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2007.09.002
title: A transdisciplinary lexicon of complexity for educational science
description: The article proposes a new lexicon needed for a complexity-based science of education, containing concepts such as '(causal) reciprocal interaction,' 'interactivity,' 'connectivity,' and 'generativity', together with 'complexity' itself and its nonlinear dynamics including 'bootstrapping', 'multiplier effects', and 'deviation-amplifying effects'. It also discusses expanded notions of causality, from triadic reciprocal causation to web-like causal structures and Juarrero's reconfiguration of cause to include bottom-up and emergent top-down structures.
requirements: Researchers must develop new tools of thought to go beyond trained thinking in terms of linear causality

policy makers

article_title: Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models
citation: Peng Wang, Fred Paas. (2026). Five Educational-Psychology Lenses for Training and Evaluating AI Models. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10195-8
title: Training data functions as a hidden curriculum that socializes AI models into the values and biases implicit in their corpus
description: The article extends the educational concept of the hidden curriculum to AI: "In the context of AI, the training data serves as a hidden curriculum for the model (Bender et al., 2021)." Models trained on open internet text learn patterns reflecting societal biases, stereotypes, and power structures, effectively socializing them into the worldview implicit in the corpus. This motivates auditing and curating datasets and treating feedback loops as value-laden pedagogical signals.
requirements: Developers must audit teacher signals, including labelers and training data, because models derive behavior from human-generated examples and judgments
constraints: The socialization is functional rather than conscious, and the analogy risks oversimplifying because AI does not develop genuine understanding or independent moral reasoning
target_learners: AI developers and dataset curators
educational researchers studying AI alignment
target_learning_goals: Recognizing and mitigating implicit bias and norms transmitted to models through training data and feedback
examples: The article notes that an LLM trained on open internet text learns societal biases, spurring work on auditing and curating datasets to educate the AI more fairly
