article_title: Emotional Wellbeing in the Context of Primary-Secondary School Transitions: A Concept Analysis Paper
citation: Bagnall, C. L., Jindal-Snape, D., Banwell, E., Panayiotou, M., Mason, C., & Qualter, P. (2025). Emotional Wellbeing in the Context of Primary-Secondary School Transitions: A Concept Analysis Paper. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09990-6
title: Conceptual model of emotional wellbeing in the context of primary-secondary school transitions with three defining attributes
description: The paper's central contribution is a concept analysis (Walker and Avant, 2005 method) defining emotional wellbeing in the context of primary-secondary school transitions as a distinct construct. Its defining attributes are that it includes "children's affective experience of navigating primary-secondary school transitions, in the here-and-now", children's evaluations of their emotional functioning globally and in specific social, academic, environmental, and personal transition domains, and children's perceptions of their internal and external resources to manage transition demands and maintain a stable affective state. The model is grounded in hedonia and eudaimonia perspectives and mapped onto Jindal-Snape's Multiple and Multi-dimensional Transitions Theory domains.
requirements: Conceptualisation must be developed in partnership with children to be contextually and experientially relevant, age and stage appropriate
constraints: The construct is specific to the primary-secondary school transitions context; the authors state general emotional wellbeing or transitions appraisals alone do not fully represent children's experiences during this time
target_learners: Children aged 10-14 navigating primary-secondary school transitions (Year 6/7 in England, P7/S1 in Scotland)
target_learning_goals: Emotional wellbeing during school transitions
Adaptation to multiple and multi-dimensional transition changes
examples: A fictional model case, James, a Year 7 pupil, illustrates all defining attributes: feeling excited and confident before the move, evaluating school size within a specific domain, and drawing on supportive family as an external resource

citation: Herbert W. Marsh, Jiesi Guo, Philip D. Parker, Reinhard Pekrun, Geetanjali Basarkod, Theresa Dicke, et al. (2023). Peer Victimization: an Integrative Review and Cross-National Test of a Tripartite Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09765-x
title: Tripartite model of victimization: relational, verbal, and physical components as distinct constructs
description: The tripartite model holds that peer victimization comprises three distinguishable components — relational, verbal, and physical — that relate differently to antecedents and outcomes such as gender, well-being, and anti-bullying attitudes. The article argues support for unidimensional models stems from poor measurement and inappropriate theoretical models, noting that "Marsh et al. (2011, 2022; also see Bear et al., 2014) argue for a tripartite model that distinguishes between physical, relational, and verbal components." The model is positioned against bivariate (overt vs. relational) accounts that combine verbal with physical victimization, and against global scores such as the PISA three-item composite. Cyberbullying is treated within this framework as a manifestation of relational bullying rather than a fourth component, since it "largely parallels and strongly correlates with relational bullying".
requirements: Appropriate measurement tools that yield well-differentiated, not overly highly correlated, components with discriminant validity
Statistical tools such as ESEM that allow cross-loadings rather than traditional CFA
constraints: Support for the model in victimization research has been limited because most studies use global or two-component measures

adolescents in primary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing peer victimization and bullying
protecting student well-being and mental health
shaping anti-bullying attitudes
examples: PISA2018 six victimization items mapped onto relational, verbal, and physical components and tested against five competing structural models

article_title: A Testing Load: Investigating Test Mode Effects on Test Score, Cognitive Load and Scratch Paper Use with Secondary School Students
citation: James Pengelley · Peter R. Whipp · Nina Rovis-Hermann. (2023). A Testing Load: Investigating Test Mode Effects on Test Score, Cognitive Load and Scratch Paper Use with Secondary School Students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09781-x
title: Tripartite cognitive load model applied to assessment: intrinsic, extraneous, and additive total load
description: The article draws on the tripartite model of cognitive load, in which "intrinsic load (IL) is associated with the complexity of the material being learned" and extraneous load arises from instructional design or environment rather than content. IL and EL are additive: when their combined demands exceed working memory capacity, students experience poorer test performance and comprehension. The study applies this framework to assessment, treating test mode as a manipulation of extraneous load and question difficulty as a manipulation of intrinsic load.
requirements: Assessment of mode effects requires within-subjects comparison, since the subjective experience of intrinsic load varies with individual learner characteristics such as prior knowledge and working memory capacity
constraints: Germane load has been removed from the tripartite model as a discrete type of load and incorporated into intrinsic load
The model is applied here to school-aged students completing physics revision quizzes in authentic classroom contexts
target_learners: secondary school students (year 9, aged 13–14)
target_learning_goals: physics problem-solving assessed via Ohm's Law calculation questions
examples: The study manipulated extraneous load via computer versus paper test mode and intrinsic load via four low and four high element-interactivity Ohm's Law questions validated by expert teachers

article_title: Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration
citation: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1
title: True theoretical integration as coherent synthesis grounded in an explicit meta-theory, distinct from aggregation
description: The article distinguishes true theoretical integration from mere combination of variables or measures. In the author's organismic tradition, integration means "bringing them into a truly coherent, organized whole" rather than adding elements. A genuine synthesis creates new insights and frameworks that capture the strengths and address the limitations of the integrated theories, and is grounded in a consistent set of assumptions and meta-theory. The article uses this criterion to evaluate cross-theoretical fusion efforts in the special issue, warning that fused theories may become lists of variables with unclear inclusion criteria and problematic psychometrics.
requirements: An explicit meta-theory and philosophic grounding
A solid set of links between abstract constructs and empirical data
A consistent set of priorities and aims
constraints: A model cannot integrate a theory, but a theory can integrate a model
Theories differ in integrative span; some have no business trying to integrate others
target_learners: Educational researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: Understanding how motivation theories can be legitimately combined or integrated
examples: The author evaluates AGT's combination of mastery versus performance goals with SDT's autonomy construct into a goal complex, asking whether AGT can absorb autonomy's organismic implications

description: This account holds that retention curves can be U-shaped because memory lapses "reflect periods of transition between different memory phases" (STM, ITM, LTM) with distinct kinetics and molecular requirements, or because lapses "reflect temporary failures in memory retrieval" when internal cues present during training fluctuate in the first hours after training. title: Base learning-path recommendations on learner interaction traces rather than externally engineered metadata
description: In open-ended, unstructured learning environments where learning objects lack prerequisite annotations or other metadata, a planner can still generate effective personalized learning sequences by mining patterns from the interaction traces learners leave on learning objects. The article's simulation demonstrated that such a trace-based planner could match or exceed a prerequisite-informed planner, showing that learner behaviour data implicitly encodes relationship information that would otherwise require knowledge engineering. This principle is realized by the CFLS planner's use of collaborative filtering over learning sequences.
requirements: A learning environment that captures usage data (learner identifier, learning outcome value, timestamp) attached to learning objects
Accumulated interaction data from prior learners
constraints: Requires the environment to have been in operation long enough to accumulate sufficient data
Cold start problem when little data is available
target_learners: self-directed learners in open-ended learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized sequence recommendations for learning object consumption
examples: The simulation captured P[learned] values and timestamps on each learning object as learners interacted, and the CFLS planner used only this captured data to form neighbourhoods and rank candidate paths.

citation: Gerhard Weber & Peter Brusilovsky. (2016). ELM-ART – An Interactive and Intelligent Web-Based Electronic Textbook. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0066-8
title: Traffic light metaphor for prerequisite-based adaptive navigation support
description: In an overview of course sections and pages, ELM-ART used a traffic light metaphor to show students whether a page is ready to be worked on, already learned, or not ready to be worked on. The server computed learning status from previously visited pages and whether their exercises were solved successfully, and used this status to suggest the next best page, implementing individual curriculum sequencing. article_title: Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models
citation: Morris, W., Holmes, L., Choi, J. S., & Crossley, S. (2025). Automated Scoring of Constructed Response Items in Math Assessment Using Large Language Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00418-w
title: Transformer attention-based semantic representation for automated constructed response scoring
description: The article describes how transformer LLMs such as BERT generate sentence-level embeddings through attention layers where "each embedding in the sequence is compared with and modified by each other embedding based on their similarity." This allows word meanings to be contextually influenced, producing a classification token representing the semantic meaning of the entire sequence. After finetuning, this token predicts human scores for constructed response items, capturing relationships that bag-of-words approaches miss.
requirements: Labeled training data for finetuning on specific scoring tasks
constraints: Bag-of-words approaches consider words individually outside syntactic context, limiting generalizability
target_learners: Students producing constructed responses in math assessments
target_learning_goals: Automated prediction of human scores for open-ended responses
examples: DeBERTa-v3-large was finetuned as a pseudo-regression task with MSE loss, with predicted scores rounded to the nearest integer during post-processing.

citation: Wulff, P., Mientus, L., Nowak, A., & Borowski, A. (2023). Utilizing a Pretrained Language Model (BERT) to Classify Preservice Physics Teachers' Written Reflections. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 33, 439–466. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00290-6

description: The article describes transfer learning as training "a general language representation from large language datasets" during pretraining, followed by fine-tuning on a downstream task. BERT uses a masked-token prediction objective (similar to a cloze task) and a next-sentence-prediction task during pretraining. The authors explain that "pretrained model weights in language models can form a solid backbone that provides structure for further downstream tasks", reducing the amount of task-specific training data needed.

citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Trestle model: an incremental apprentice learner model within the Apprentice Learner Architecture
description: The Trestle model is the second apprentice learner model built within the Apprentice Learner Architecture. It uses Trestle, an incremental concept learning algorithm based on psychological studies of how humans learn concepts, for when-learning. Incremental algorithms efficiently update their classification tree in response to each new datum without reprocessing all previous training examples. Like the Decision Tree model, it draws on the same small set of prior knowledge (six operators and three types of relational knowledge).
requirements: Requires tutor interactions providing steps, demonstrations, and feedback
constraints: Incremental approaches learn less accurate classifiers than non-incremental approaches because they do not reconsider all data during each update
target_learners: non-programmer tutor authors
target_learning_goals: learning expert models for tutoring systems from demonstrations and feedback
examples: Evaluated across seven additional tutoring domains alongside the Decision Tree model

description: The article characterises Transformer AI systems such as GPT-3 as "a general-purpose language machine" that works like a highly trained text completer, attending to the previous 750 words to continue text. Because "Transformers are models of language not experiential knowledge", they can produce plausible text yet invent references and studies. The article uses this account to explain both the assessment threat and the fake-reference problem.

academic researchers

citation: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6
title: Transactivity construct: 18 types of transactive moves along three dimensions
description: Transactivity is a construct from a Piagetian framework formalized as 18 types of transactive moves that characterize each student's conversational turn as an explicit reasoning display connecting with previously articulated reasoning. The article draws on three dimensions for motivating experimental studies: self-oriented versus other-oriented (whether the contribution operates on the speaker's own or a partner's reasoning), representational versus transformational (whether the original idea is restated or transformed), and consensus-oriented versus conflict-oriented. The authors propose these dimensions create a logical ordering of demand that applies to corresponding APT facilitation moves.
requirements: Reasoning must be explicitly displayed in some form for a contribution to count as a transact
constraints: Alternative frameworks (Inter-subjective Meaning Making, Productive Agency) privilege subtly different formulations of similar behaviors
target_learners: collaborative learning group members across grade levels
target_learning_goals: explicit articulation of reasoning
building on partners' reasoning
mutual examination and integration of mental models
examples: The article uses the self/other-oriented and representational/transformational dimensions to characterize APT moves such as Revoice (self-oriented, transformational) and Agree/Disagree (other-oriented, representational, conflict-oriented)

title: AES research should report thorough and transparent performance protocols to enable fair comparison and replication
description: The article advocates that AES studies describe methodologies and report outcomes under proper protocols, because present reports "commonly – and perhaps inadvertently – lack transparency", hindering performance evaluation and comparison of techniques. Transparent reporting should include agreement metrics computed by consistent procedures, per-dataset (per writing task) results, and disclosure of which data splits were used, permitting fairer comparisons among AES systems and study replication.

Disclosure of training/testing data availability and splits

article_title: Assessing multiple object tracking in young children using a game
citation: Kimiko Ryokai, Faraz Farzin, Eric Kaltman, Greg Niemeyer. (2013). Assessing multiple object tracking in young children using a game. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9278-x
title: TrackFX: the first game-based MOT task on a touch tablet for children as young as 30 months
description: TrackFX is a touch-tablet game transferring the classic MOT paradigm to children under 5 in non-experimental settings. Players track ladybug targets among spider distractors hidden under leaf occluders that move randomly at "a normalized velocity of 540 px/sec for 10 s" before the player selects the leaf covering each target. Levels follow a 2-up-1-down psychophysical staircase, advancing at or above 66% correct twice in a row and dropping otherwise, with a 66% tracking threshold estimated from each session.
requirements: Children must understand the rule of identifying target ladybugs and find the task engaging for the task to measure true tracking ability
constraints: Levels 1–3 are introductory acclimation levels, not included in data analyses
target_learners: children 30–58 months old
target_learning_goals: multiple object tracking and selective visual attention
examples: Deployed at the UC Berkeley Harold E. Jones Child Study Center during regular choice-time, where all 31 children successfully played it

article_title: Managing large classes in virtual teaching: experiences of university teachers in Ghana during COVID-19
citation: Inusah Salifu · Usman Kojo Abonyi. (2023). Managing large classes in virtual teaching: experiences of university teachers in Ghana during COVID-19. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10151-7
title: Moore's Theory of Transactional Distance (dialogue, structure, learner-autonomy)
description: The study's theoretical framework is Moore's Theory of Transactional Distance, which holds that distance in distance education is "transactional, not spatial or temporal" — a psychological and communication space between learner and teacher. Success of virtual teaching depends on three transactions: dialogue (quality interactions creating knowledge), course structure (rigidity or flexibility of objectives, assessment modes, teacher- versus learner-centredness), and learner-autonomy, which is determined by the first two. The theory provided the framework for analysing teacher-student-environment interplay and framed interview questions and observation memos.
requirements: Virtual teaching programmes must attend to dialogue, course structure, and learner autonomy for success
constraints: The theory posits a contrary relationship among the three transactions: an increase in one may cause a corresponding decrease in the other two
target_learners: university students in virtual large classes
target_learning_goals: effective instructor-learner interaction
self-directed learning
well-structured course content
examples: The study used the TTD's dialogue, structure and learner-autonomy elements to code interview data and structure classroom observations

article_title: Touch Arithmetic: A process-based Computer-Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics
citation: Adesina, A., Stone, R., Batmaz, F., & Jones, I. (2014). Touch Arithmetic: A process‐based Computer‐Aided Assessment approach for capture of problem solving steps in the context of elementary mathematics.
title: Trace-based capture of problem-solving process for process-level assessment and feedback
description: The article proposes using structured trace information, analogous to on-line requirement traceability in software engineering, to capture problem-solving steps. As students perform interactive actions on an integrated problem text and solution space, dependency links are created between solution items and their origins, allowing an answer's life to be followed "in both forward and backward directions". This makes the thinking behind a solution visible and supports process-level feedback, which the article cites Hattie and Timperley as arguing is most effective in assessment situations.
requirements: Interactive problem-solving tasks that reduce inconsistencies and ambiguities in the representation of solution steps
Integration of the problem text/scenario with the solution space so interactive actions are executed between them
constraints: Fewer prior studies had explored dependencies and relationships in the problem-solving process in ways they can be unambiguously represented, motivating this approach
target_learners: primary school children learning elementary mathematics
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of strengths and weaknesses in problem solving
process-level feedback on strategies and intermediate steps
examples: The MuTAT prototype implements the approach: dragging numbers from problem pane to solution pane creates trace links, and a diagrammatic representation of solution steps is generated from the recorded traces

article_title: Can tablet apps support the learning of handwriting? An investigation of learning outcomes in kindergarten classroom
citation: Nathalie Bonneton-Botté, Sylvain Fleury, Nathalie Girard, Maëlys Le Magadou, Anthony Cherbonnier, Mickaël Renault, Eric Anquetil, Eric Jamet. (2020). Can Tablet Apps Support the Learning of Handwriting? An Investigation of Learning Outcomes in Kindergarten Classroom. Computers and Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103831
title: Deliver augmented handwriting feedback on completion of each trial so it does not interrupt the writing movement
description: In motor learning of handwriting, knowledge of results should be delivered at the end of a trial rather than the moment an error occurs, so that feedback does not break the child's writing gesture or encoding process. The Kaligo app operationalizes this: feedback "was systematically delivered on completion of each letter, so as not to interrupt the child's activity". The authors contrast this with a prior app that gave feedback as soon as an error was made, which they believed may have disrupted encoding, and with teachers' typically delayed feedback.
requirements: Automatic analysis of the written product (shape, direction, stroke order, continuity) so feedback can be computed and delivered immediately after each trial
constraints: The article states the medium-level benefit cannot be attributed to any single factor; real-time feedback is one candidate among several (one-to-one instruction, dynamic model, appeal of tablets)
target_learners: kindergarten beginning writers learning cursive handwriting
target_learning_goals: legibility and kinematic quality of cursive letter production, transferable to paper
examples: Kaligo displayed a colored horseshoe gauge with size feedback (pink rectangles) immediately after each completed letter or word

citation: Caballero-Julia, D., Martín-Lucas, J., & Andrade-Silva, L. E. (2024). Unpacking the relationship between screen use and educational outcomes in childhood: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105049
title: Tri-phasic periodisation of childhood screen research as an organising framework for the field.
description: This framework organises the scientific literature on childhood screen use into three publication periods identified through MANOVA-Biplot analysis of a lexical matrix built from 158 article abstracts. The framework provides a historical perspective intended to guide future research.

constraints: Based exclusively on the Scopus database; exclusion of other databases could limit the breadth of the literature reviewed

policymakers

citation: Gobodwana, A., 2024, 'The strategies in teaching isiXhosa semantics in Foundation Phase: A systematic review', Reading & Writing 15(1), a493. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v15i1.493
title: Translanguaging as a practical theory of language for multilingual classrooms
description: Translanguaging is presented as a broader understanding of bilingualism and multilingualism that departs from traditional approaches to language learning. The article distinguishes it from code-switching: "while code-switching involves adhering to unique grammatical rules for each language, translanguaging revolves around the practical use of language in multilingual communication". Following Wei (2018), its primary goal is to foster bilingualism and multilingualism rather than replacing children's first language, and it values the unique resources of multilingual speakers by blurring boundaries between languages.

constraints: The article states translanguaging is not an official pedagogical approach to learning in South African classrooms

citation: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456
title: Transformative Learning Theory as an adult learning framework centered on critical reflection on experience
description: Transformative Learning Theory, introduced by Jack Mezirow in 1975, frames learning as making meaning of experience through critical reflection, and the article uses it both as a reviewed application and as one of four focal teaching methods. It also distinguishes informative from transformative learning, citing Kegan: "informative learning changes what we know; transformative learning cha nges how we know". In the meta-analysis it produced the highest attitude effect size (d=1,4760) for Biology pre-service teachers.

Critical reflection on assumptions, which the article says can occur "either in group interaction or independently"
constraints: The article describes it as "a uniquely adult form of metacognitive reasoning", so the framework is scoped to adult learners
The article notes assumptions "can be changed only after critical reflection"
target_learners: Pre-service teachers
Adult learners
target_learning_goals: Changes in understanding of self
Revision of belief systems
Changes in lifestyle
examples: The reviewed study by Çimen (2013) applied a transformative learning model based on environmental education with pre-service biology teachers

citation: Stelling H, Burford B, Park S, McGurk L, Brown M E L, Vance G. (2026). How do doctors build knowledge around obstetric emergencies? A scoping review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2026-119725

description: The review's organising framework maps knowledge-building for obstetric emergencies onto three domains: "training reflected structured and formal approaches to knowledge acquisition; context encompassed both local workplace realities and wider systemic influences; and experience captured knowledge developed through clinical encounters". Knowledge flows within and across domains through an interplay of knowledge "received" from published sources, colleagues, educators and patients and knowledge "embodied" through personal clinical experience and practice. The framework was generated inductively from 369 included sources and used to structure the synthesis and its recommendations.

The framework deliberately focuses on positive attributes, in line with a positive psychology perspective, because the included first-order meta-analyses predominantly examined positive traits.

title: Tripathy et al framework of three categories of simulated manikin death
description: The review cites a theoretical framework of simulated manikin death developed through a mixed-methods approach, outlining three categories by which manikin death may occur in a simulation session: 'expected death' (both facilitators and participants know death should be expected), 'unexpected death' (only participants are unaware), and 'death due to inaction/action' (death determined by participants' actions). constraints: The review presents the framework as background from adult and general simulation literature, not as tested within the three included paediatric studies
target_learners: healthcare professionals in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: preparing learners for death of patients in clinical practice
managing emotional responses during resuscitation scenarios
examples: The review introduces the framework when discussing how death of the manikin could feasibly occur in a variety of scenarios

title: TRI 15-minute session structure of Rereading for Fluency, Word Work, and Guided Oral Reading across four instructional levels
description: Each TRI session is composed of three instructional activities that build on one another so the student reaches fluent reading with beginning comprehension. Strategies vary across four progressively more challenging instructional levels (pink, blue, green, purple), and teachers use the TRI Diagnostic Map to plan and chart daily progress and select texts matched to the student's instructional reading level.

segmenting, blending, and phoneme–grapheme relations
defining and using tier 1 and tier 2 vocabulary
beginning comprehension strategies such as summarizing, predicting, and making inferences

description: The article describes a traditional ITS model consisting of three main components: the domain model, which "comprises the learning content, instruction topics, and the relationships among topics"; the student model, which stores information such as learning level, history, preferences, and goals and monitors learning processes; and the teaching model, which provides feedback about student progress and guidance about proceeding to the most appropriate learning task. citation: Wendi Mizer Stachler, R. Brent Young, Mari Borr. (2013). Sustainability of professional development to enhance student achievement: A shift in the professional development paradigm. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(4), 13-30. https://www.jae-online.org
title: Transtheoretical model of behavior change as a framework for teacher professional development sustainability
description: The article applies Prochaska's transtheoretical model of behavior change to teacher adoption of integrated curricula. The model "addressed five stages of change: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, and maintenance," with a sixth, rarely attained termination stage in which a person maintains the desired behavior without hesitation or temptation. The authors use the model to interpret sustained lesson use: teachers continuing to use Science-in-CTE materials a year later are read as having reached the maintenance stage, and they argue that understanding the model could lead to increased professional growth and student achievement in CTE programs.
requirements: Teachers must move through the stages of change for pedagogical change to be sustained; beliefs, attitudes, and investment on the teacher's part are described as vital to implementing and maintaining change
constraints: The termination stage is described as more often unattained
target_learners: secondary agricultural education teachers
secondary science teachers
target_learning_goals: sustained use of integrated science-enhanced pedagogy
integration of core academic content into CTE curricula
examples: The authors interpret 92% of experimental agricultural education teachers as having attained the maintenance phase because they continued using the lessons and model one year after the pilot study

title: Tricomponent view of reading attitude (cognitive, affective, conative)
description: The article adopts Mathewson's tricomponent view of attitude, in which attitude comprises evaluation as the cognitive component, feeling as the affective component, and action readiness as the conative component. article_title: Evidence-Based Literacy Support: The "Literacy Octopus" Trial. Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Pippa Lord, Adam Rabiasz, Palak Roy, Jennie Harland, Ben Styles, Katherine Fowler. (2017). Evidence-based literacy support: the 'Literacy Octopus' trial — Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN84508118
title: Pair disseminated evidence-based materials with support that transforms them into practice and builds school implementation conditions
description: The trial's process evaluation indicates that disseminating research evidence, whether passively or with added active support, did not change attainment, so providers of research evidence need to focus on transforming the research so it can easily be applied in practice. Implementation factors the report highlights include the conditions within the school for engaging with evidence and adopting new approaches, in-school collaboration, further enquiry, and trying out, reviewing, adapting and embedding approaches. requirements: Research must be transformed so it can easily be applied in practice, per the report's recommendation to providers of research evidence
constraints: The report states school and teacher time was not measured but was a challenge for some schools, both for initial engagement and time to implement evidence-based strategies

target_learning_goals: Key Stage 2 literacy attainment
teachers' use of research evidence in teaching practice
examples: The CEM active arm added twilight CPD sessions, use of the InCAS pupil diagnostic tool, and teacher peer observation between sessions on top of the evidence-based materials booklet and posters

citation: Saman Ebadi, Khadijeh Davood Ghuchi. (2018). Investigating the Effects of Blended Learning Approach on Vocabulary Enhancement from EFL Learners' Perspectives. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 8 No. 2, April - June 2018.
title: Transactional Distance Theory as the theoretical basis for blended learning
description: The article presents Transactional Distance Theory (TDT), first proposed by Michael G. Moore in 1970, as "a theory behind the blended learning". TDT analyzes teaching and learning as the separation between learners and between teachers and learners in distance education, a "psychological and communications space" that is bridged through course structure, learner autonomy, and dialogue. The study uses this framework to motivate combining face-to-face teaching with asynchronous online app-based learning.
requirements: The theory presumes distance education settings where separation between teachers and learners must be bridged
target_learners: Iranian EFL learners at intermediate (CEFR B) proficiency in higher education
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge
examples: The study operationalized the theory in a supplemental blended model: face-to-face classroom teaching plus asynchronous Memrise use outside scheduled class time

citation: Danica Veselinov, Radmila Nikolić. (2015). THE POSSIBILITIES OF ENCOURAGING STUDENT'S METACOGNITIVE STRATEGIES THROUGH HEURISTIC-METHODOLOGICAL INSTRUCTION. https://doi.org/10.17810/2015.06

connecting new content with prior knowledge

effective parenting
parental school involvement

constraints: The section on evaluating evolutionary relationships was revised because earlier students had room for improvement on resolved and polytomous relatedness items

description: The article's organizing framework distinguishes personality traits from social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills by mode of assessment rather than content: "traits refer to a person's typical or average performance, skills refer to their capacity or maximal performance." Distinguishing malleable SEB skills from stable personality traits for intervention design
examples: The article contrasts an introverted person's typical quietness with their capacity to "turn it on" and engage a room full of strangers when the situation calls for it

title: Transactional distance: online learning distance is social and relational, determined by dialogue and structure
description: The review presents Moore's transactional distance concept as the first foundational concept of online learning: distance is not physical but "a social, psychological, and relational distance between teachers and learners that is fluid and manageable based on a function of dialogue and structure." Increasing meaningful dialogue reduces it; structure means the rigidity or flexibility of the educational program. The review applies this to online course design in medical education.
requirements: Educators must design ongoing dialogue between teacher and learners and accommodate individual students' needs rather than rely on the communication medium itself.
constraints: The review states the medium of communication would not automatically close the distance between teachers and students; highly structured teaching with minimal dialogue yields high transactional distance.
target_learners: medical students in online or distance learning

title: Preparing and educating trainers to address misplaced patient concerns and build confidence is a worthwhile investment for SCIG adoption
description: The article recommends investing in preparing and educating trainers who deliver SCIG training to patients. article_title: The Virtual Operative Assistant: An explainable artificial intelligence tool for simulation-based training in surgery and medicine.
citation: Mirchi N, Bissonnette V, Yilmaz R, Ledwos N, Winkler-Schwartz A, Del Maestro RF. (2020). The Virtual Operative Assistant: An explainable artificial intelligence tool for simulation-based training in surgery and medicine. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0229596
title: Transparency framework for explainable artificial intelligence in simulation-based training
description: The article introduces a framework in which a simulated task generates raw data, metrics of performance are created and selected for their ability to differentiate groups, and a machine learning algorithm is trained and tested to build an educational feedback platform. New users' normalized metrics yield both a group classification and "an individual breakdown of metric performance", so the learner sees how each metric contributes to the model's decision. The framework is presented as flexible: it "can be employed to teach any form of complex task where a multivariate dataset can be obtained from experts and non-experts".
requirements: A labelled dataset containing a relatively large number of users, normalized metrics, and a trained predictive model whose weights can be exposed to the learner
constraints: The validated implementation uses a linear SVM distinguishing only two groups of expertise; the model bias is a weight without a corresponding metric and is left out of metric-wise assessment
target_learners: Surgical and medical trainees (residents, fellows, medical students)
target_learning_goals: Complex psychomotor technical skills, e.g. neurosurgical tumor resection
examples: The framework was validated by building the Virtual Operative Assistant for a virtual reality subpial brain tumor resection task on the NeuroVR simulator

title: Transformative learning theory applied through consumer co-delivery as the workshop's mechanism of attitude change
description: The workshop was designed around transformative learning theory, in which "learners radically change their existing beliefs and understandings through reflection on how they were originally learned and practical experience; exposure to and empathy with alternative viewpoints; discourse in a supportive environment". Rather than didactic skills teaching, the design sought to promote conceptual change by activating prior understandings, featuring consumer-led "Conversations about breathlessness" sessions, and linking chronic breathlessness to chronic pain science. The authors identify this biopsychosocial focus and consumer involvement as the facilitators of the observed attitude and confidence changes.
requirements: Sessions that activate participants' prior understandings through reflection and description before introducing new concepts
Exposure to and empathy with alternative viewpoints, operationalised here through conversations led by people living with chronic breathlessness
constraints: Evidence for the mechanism is limited to immediate post-workshop self-reported attitude, familiarity and confidence change in a single-group evaluation without a control condition
target_learners: Health professionals (nursing and allied health clinicians) working with people with chronic breathlessness
target_learning_goals: Biopsychosocial understanding of chronic breathlessness
Person-centred assessment and non-pharmacological management of chronic breathlessness
Critical reflection on own beliefs and expectations about breathlessness
examples: The 3-day workshop combined presentations of research evidence with consumer-led conversation sessions, interactive practice with multidimensional breathlessness assessment tools, and reflection on participants' own beliefs and expectations

Journal of Youth and Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-019-01184-y
title: Transactional model of adolescent development applied to relationships, school well-being, and achievement
description: The article applies Sameroff's transactional model, under which "adolescent development is a product of the continuous dynamic interactions between adolescents and the experiences provided by their social settings (e.g., parents, friends, teachers)". Its core is the interdependent, reciprocal effects of adolescent and environment: socialization effects run from relationship quality to well-being, while evocative effects run from well-being to relationship quality. The study's cross-lagged results supported this reciprocity during the transition to lower secondary school.
requirements: Longitudinal cross-lagged data capturing both directions of association (socialization and evocative effects) across the transition
constraints: The article states the analyses were correlational, which inhibits confident assertions on causality
target_learners: Early adolescents (mean age 12.3 at outset) undergoing the primary-to-lower-secondary school transition
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement during educational transitions
School well-being (satisfaction and stress)
examples: Cross-lagged SEMs over three time points (grade 6 fall, grade 7 fall, grade 7 spring) with 848 Finnish adolescents supported reciprocal paths in both directions

article_title: The power of simulation: a large-scale narrative analysis of learners' experiences.
citation: Bearman Margaret, Greenhill Jennene, Nestel Debra. (2019). The power of simulation: a large‐scale narrative analysis of learners’ experiences. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13747
title: Transformative learning theory used as a sensitising notion, with the 'event-story' as the unit of narrative analysis
description: The article draws on Mezirow's transformative learning theory — the transformation of frames of reference through critical reflection — as a sensitising notion: "Within this study, we use transformative learning theory as a sensitising notion", shaping design and analysis without making it a study of transformation itself. Narratives are analysed as 'event-stories' following Sandberg, with Reese et al.'s three coherence dimensions of context, chronology and theme. The theory frames the contrast between progress narratives and the rarer transformation narratives.
requirements: Analysts must be sensitised to the possibility of transformations prior to conceptualising the work, as the authors describe
constraints: The authors state this is not a study of transformative learning, but of narratives regarding powerful learning experiences involving SBE
target_learners: Health professional educators reflecting on their simulation learning experiences
target_learning_goals: Understanding how SBE may influence learning, identity and frames of reference
examples: Transformation narratives such as T25, where a simulated death led to a lasting shift in how the nurse understood her own voice
